report.title: Structural assessment report
report.generatedBy: Generated by DamageScale — AI structural damage assessment (demo)

scale.title: The three collapse classes
scale.intro: Every photo is classified into one of three collapse classes, from a standing structure to rubble. The classes come from PHI-Net's Collapse Mode task, which grades a building by how much of its structural system survived rather than by cosmetic appearance.

details.nonCollapse: The structural system is intact. Damage, where present, is confined to finishes: surface cracking, spalled render, broken glazing. Load paths are continuous. Note that this class covers minor damage as well as none.
details.partialCollapse: One or more structural elements have failed — a floor slab, a bay, a section of load-bearing wall — while the remaining frame still carries load. Progressive collapse is the governing risk.
details.globalCollapse: The primary structural system has failed. What remains reads as debris rather than frame. Assessment shifts from repair to demolition and site clearance.

dataset.title: Dataset and labeling
dataset.sourcesBody: The imagery comes from PHI-Net, the post-hazard image dataset published by the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center (PEER) at UC Berkeley. This project uses Task 5, Collapse Mode. The split used for training holds 1,226 training images — 322 non-collapse, 379 partial collapse, 525 global collapse — and 146 validation images (39 / 40 / 67). The classes are imbalanced toward global collapse, which is worth weighing when reading per-class results.
dataset.labelingBody: Labels ship with PHI-Net rather than being annotated here, so the grading criteria are the dataset authors'. Their definition matters for reading results: non-collapse means intact OR minor damage with the structure still standing — not undamaged. Partial collapse means part of the structure failed while the rest stands; global collapse means the primary structural system failed.

model.title: Model architecture
model.body: Two classifiers are trained and selectable at prediction time. The first is ResNet50 with ImageNet transfer learning, taking 224×224 input with Caffe-style preprocessing (BGR channel order, ImageNet mean subtraction, no standard-deviation division). The second is a YOLO11 nano classifier trained on the same three-class split for comparison.
model.frameworkNote: The two models run on different frameworks — TensorFlow and PyTorch — behind one predict() interface, so the app never knows which is active. A third slot is registered and waiting for a further model.
model.mockNote: A deterministic mock backend remains available for environments without the model weights installed, so the demo still runs anywhere. It is labeled as the mock in the model picker and never impersonates a trained model.

metrics.title: Evaluation metrics
metrics.intro: Headline accuracy is measured; the per-class breakdown below is not filled in yet and is shown as pending rather than estimated.
metrics.confusionCaption: Empty 3×3 confusion-matrix slot. Rows are actual classes, columns are predicted classes; the diagonal cells carry each class's color at low opacity. Counts will be filled in once a per-class evaluation is exported.
metrics.accuracyNote: Validation top-1 accuracy on the same three-class split, so the figures are directly comparable.

gradcam.title: What is the heatmap?
gradcam.body: The heatmap is generated with Grad-CAM, a technique that traces the model's prediction back to the image regions that influenced it most. Warm zones mark where the model looked when grading the damage — cracked walls, failed columns, collapsed sections — so you can verify the verdict rests on structural evidence, not on the background.
gradcam.tryNote: On the <link>analyze page</link>, use the heatmap toggle to overlay it on any result.
